assistant.content: Non-modal variables mean that the value is not retained after each program block is executed; it must be redefined on the next call. Modal variable values remain until modified or the program ends. If you are worried about confusing variables in milling tool compensation, you can use local variables #1 to #33 to define non-modal values, ensuring that each subroutine call resets them to avoid conflicts.

user.content: I see, so using local variables can avoid the problem of non-modal variable residue? Then are system variables in the #5000 series modal? How should I choose variable types during actual machining?

assistant.content: Yes, local variables are non-modal by default and are automatically cleared each time a subroutine is called. System variables #5000+ are modal and are used to store machine tool states such as tool compensation values. Suggestion: use local variables (#1~#33) for temporary calculations, common variables (#100~#199) for passing values across programs, and system variables for machine tool parameters. You can first test with local variables in a milling compensation scenario, and once it works correctly, switch to system variables to solidify the parameters.
